The co-operative owns the shaft, the gallery, the vault and the indemnity fund, and is
composed entirely of the forty people it owns them against. Every member holds one share and
one vote. It is a genuinely democratic institution and it behaves, from below, exactly like a
landlord, because the votes that matter were taken years ago and what reaches the gallery
floor now is a steward with a board and a signature.

The dissent is not a faction and has no name, which is what makes it dangerous to the board.
Roughly a third of the membership - the younger half of the gallery, the ones with no
service years to lose - want the Kestrel core lifted and the shaft valued, on the plain
arithmetic that a valued shaft sold to an off-moon operator would pay each of them more than
thirty years of co-op wages. The board's answer has never been that they are wrong. It has
been that a sale ends the co-op, and the co-op is the only thing on Nix that has to keep them
alive when they are old.

The sealing order is the board winning that argument by making it moot. You cannot value what
you cannot reach.
